## 2 Corinthians 2 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — *"So I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you."*

- The chapter division is widely considered poor — Paul continues his explanation from chapter 1 of why he changed his travel plans. He "determined" (Greek *krino*, to decide firmly) not to come again in sorrow. The "again" implies a previous visit that had been painful. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-2-commentary; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Ellicott**: Paul "consulted his own feelings ('for myself') as well as theirs." If he had carried out his original plan, another painful visit would have been "the almost inevitable result." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Paul was defending himself against critics who said he was unreliable and fickle because he changed his travel plans. His change was pastoral care, not fickleness — he wanted to spare them another sorrowful confrontation. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-2/)
- **Precept Austin** notes MacArthur's view: Paul was referring to a painful earlier visit (not the founding visit of Acts 18) when someone openly insulted him and the Corinthians did not defend him. That prompted the "severe letter." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-2-commentary)

### v. 2 — *"For if I grieve you, who is left to cheer me but those whom I have grieved?"*

- **Ellicott**: The "for" carries a hidden argument: Paul had been accused of not caring about giving pain when he wrote sharply. His answer is that "the pain which I inflict gives to him who suffers it the power of giving me joy, and so works out an ample compensation." The abrupt question and the use of the singular number show Paul has the one great offender (the incestuous man of 1 Corinthians 5:1) before his mind's eye. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Paul knew another painful visit would not be good for him either. He thought it best to give the Corinthians "a little room" and space to repent rather than rebuking them constantly. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-2/)
- **Precept Austin (Wiersbe)**: Paul did not want to visit as a stern father but as a loving friend. If he made them sorry, how could they in turn make him glad? He wanted to give them time to make matters right. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-2-commentary)

### v. 3 — *"I wrote as I did so that on my arrival I would not be saddened by those who ought to make me rejoice..."*

- **Ellicott**: The pronoun "this very thing" shows how certain passages in his first letter were stamped on Paul's memory. His motive in writing so sharply was "to avoid giving and receiving pain when he came in person." He wanted a visit of unmixed joy. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Paul wisely understood a letter was better than a personal visit — it could show his heart without giving as much opportunity for relationship deterioration. It would give them room to repent. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-2/)
- **Precept Austin (Broomall)**: Paul indicates three reasons for writing: (1) to prepare them for his visit (v.3); (2) to manifest his love (v.4); (3) to test their obedience (v.9). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-2-commentary)

### v. 4 — *"For through many tears I wrote you out of great distress and anguish of heart, not to grieve you but to let you know how much I love you."*

- **Ellicott**: Paul remembers "the intensity of his feelings, pain that such words should be needed, anxiety as to their issue, the very tears which then, as at other times (Acts 20:19, 31; 2 Tim 1:4), were the outflow of strong emotion." Those indignant at his stern words should see in them "the strongest proof of his abounding love." The word for "anguish" (*synoche*) may reflect medical terminology — "like a tight pressure or constriction of the heart." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Paul did not enjoy confronting the Corinthians — it was hard for him. "St. Paul's Epistles were written rather with tears than with ink" (Trapp). The goal was not to grieve them but to show love. Spurgeon is quoted: "Where I have known that there existed a measure of disaffection to myself, I have not recognised it… but have acted towards the opposing person with all the more courtesy and friendliness." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-2/)
- **Precept Austin**: This was the "severe letter" — often thought to be a lost letter between 1 and 2 Corinthians, though some identify it with 1 Corinthians itself. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-2-commentary)

### v. 5 — *"Now if anyone has caused grief, he has not grieved me but all of you—to some degree, not to overstate it."*

- **Ellicott**: Three possible interpretations of the ambiguous Greek: (1) The simplest — "it is not I alone whom he hath grieved, but… all of you." They were the greatest sufferers from the scandal. Paul will not name the man; he is "a man," "such a one." The Greek makes "me he hath not grieved" emphatic. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Paul displays pastoral wisdom by not naming the man. This is probably the same man from 1 Corinthians 5 — the incestuous man living with his stepmother. The phrase "such a man" is used in both books. Some commentators disagree and think it was someone who insulted Paul personally during the "painful visit," but v.10 suggests Paul expected the Corinthians to forgive first — implying the offense was primarily against the church, not Paul personally. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-2/)
- **Gill**: The grief was caused not just to Paul but to the whole church, making greater severity necessary. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/2.htm)

### v. 6 — *"The punishment imposed on him by the majority is sufficient for him."*

- **Ellicott**: "Punishment" (Greek *epitimia*) means "censure" or "rebuke" — a different word from that used of eternal punishment. The discipline followed the pattern of 1 Corinthians 5:3-5: a meeting was held, the man was delivered to Satan, and excommunication followed. The decision was "by the majority" — it was not unanimous; a minority resisted, possibly the Judaising "Cephas" party or the party of license. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: The church discipline worked — the man apparently repented. But the Corinthians then swung to the opposite extreme and would not receive him back. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-2/)
- **Gill**: Excommunication was the punishment; the man had been humbled and brought to repentance, so nothing more was needed. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/2.htm)

### v. 7 — *"So instead, you ought to forgive and comfort him, so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow."*

- **Ellicott**: Paul's indignation had passed into "pity and anxiety." He feared the man might be "swallowed up" — suicide, madness, or apostasy seem to "float before his mind as but too possible results." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: They were just as wrong to withhold forgiveness from the repentant as they had been to tolerate his sin. "There may be a judicial forgiveness which is hard, and leaves the soul always conscious of the past. Comfort takes the soul to heart, and forgets. That is how God forgives" (Morgan). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-2/)
- **Precept Austin**: Paul's instruction is to both forgive *and* comfort — not just one or the other. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-2-commentary)
- **Gill**: The man should be forgiven "lest he should be overwhelmed with sorrow, and be reduced to despair." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/2.htm)

### v. 8 — *"Therefore I urge you to reaffirm your love for him."*

- **Ellicott**: The word for "confirm" (Greek *kyroo*, "ratify") suggests an act "as formal and public as the rebuke had been." The excommunicated man was to be re-admitted by a collective act of the Church. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Since the man repented, it was time for "love and healing." "When the offender is made to feel that, while his sin is punished, he himself is loved; and that the end aimed at is not his suffering but his good, he is more likely to be brought to repentance" (Hodge). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-2/)

### v. 9 — *"My purpose in writing you was to see if you would stand the test and be obedient in everything."*

- **Ellicott**: The Greek tense could be an "epistolary aorist," meaning Paul writes *now* to test their obedience in forgiving as they were obedient before in punishing. "It scarcely seems like St. Paul to make the punishment a trial of obedience. There is a characteristic subtle delicacy of thought in his suggesting that, having shown obedience in punishing they should show it also in forgiving." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Paul tested them: would they find it easier to obey when he asked them to be "tough" than when he asked them to show love and restoration? (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-2/)
- **Precept Austin**: "Test" (*dokime*) was used of testing metal coins for genuineness. Partial obedience is disobedience — they had obeyed by disciplining but now needed to obey by loving. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-2-commentary)

### v. 10 — *"If you forgive anyone, I also forgive him. And if I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven it in the presence of Christ for your sake."*

- **Ellicott**: Paul is recalling the procedure of 1 Corinthians 5:3-7 — though absent in body, he had shared spiritually in the censure; now he anticipates sharing in the absolution. "In the person of Christ" (literally "in the face of Christ") means Christ was acting in or by him. Paul claims "in its fulness the authority given to the Apostles of Christ in John 20:23." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: The offending man had also sinned against Paul in some way, but Paul expected the Corinthians to take the lead in forgiveness. Even in discipline, believers are to treat the disciplined person with love, as they would an unbeliever — hoping to win them. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-2/)
- **Ligonier (Reformed)**: The Corinthians had obeyed Paul's harsher letter and disciplined the man. Lovingly restoring him would be their new act of obedience. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/knowing-satans-designs)

### v. 11 — *"...in order that Satan should not outwit us. For we are not unaware of his schemes."*

- **Ellicott**: The imagery is of a game against the Tempter where souls are the stakes. Paul's last move was to deliver the sinner to Satan for his ultimate deliverance, but Satan might outwit them by tempting the sinner to despair. "Stratagem must be met by strategy." Paul's wide experience — buffeted by Satan's messenger (2 Cor 12:7), hindered in his work (1 Thess 2:18) — taught him how the Tempter could turn "even the rules of an ascetic rigour, or the remorse of a sin-burdened conscience, into an occasion of yet further and more irremediable sin." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "Take advantage" (Greek *pleonekteo*) means to cheat someone out of what belongs to them — peace, joy, fellowship, forgiveness, victory. Satan's strategy against the sinner: first lust, then despair. Against the church: first toleration of evil, then undue severity. Against Paul: stress to drain his effectiveness. "There is nothing more dangerous than to give Satan a chance of reducing a sinner to despair" (Calvin). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-2/)
- **Ligonier (Reformed)**: Satan wants to sow discord among believers by setting forgiven sinners against one another. "When we do not forgive and restore professing believers who have repented, we risk giving the devil a foothold in our churches." Chrysostom noted Paul's silence about the man's crime because "the time had now come to forgive." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/knowing-satans-designs)

### v. 12 — *"Now when I went to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ and a door stood open for me in the Lord..."*

- **Ellicott**: Paul returns to the narrative interrupted by vv.5-11. A church had probably been founded in Troas by Luke, but Paul's first visit had been brief. Now he comes "for the gospel's sake." "A door was opened" means opportunities for mission-work (cf. 1 Corinthians 16:9). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Paul was interested in ministering where God opened doors. "Where the master sets up a light, there is some work to be done" (Trapp). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-2/)

### v. 13 — *"I had no peace in my spirit, because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I said goodbye to them and went on to Macedonia."*

- **Ellicott**: Paul had sent Titus to Corinth to learn the effects of the first epistle, and Titus was to return to him at Troas. Not finding him, Paul's "eager anxiety" drove him to leave Troas despite the open door and hasten into Macedonia — probably to Philippi, where he met Titus. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Even with an open door, Paul felt he needed Titus. He did not regard himself as a one-man show. Verses 14-17 through 7:4 are sometimes called "the great digression" — Paul resumes the narrative of meeting Titus at 2 Corinthians 7:5. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-2/)

### v. 14 — *"But thanks be to God, who always leads us triumphantly as captives in Christ and through us spreads everywhere the fragrance of the knowledge of Him."*

- **Ellicott (decisive on translation)**: "There is absolutely no authority for the factitive meaning given to the verb in the English version" — it is not "causeth us to triumph" but "leads us in His triumph." Paul is not the triumphant commander but a captive in God's triumphal parade. The imagery is of a Roman triumph: the conqueror rides along the Via Sacra, followed by troops and prisoners, with fragrant clouds of incense. Some prisoners were executed; others were pardoned. Ellicott notes the interesting possibility that Paul wrote this around the time of Claudius's triumph over the Britons (A.D. 51), in which Caractacus figured as a prisoner — and that Claudia and Linus (2 Tim 4:21) may have been among his spared children. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Paul sees Jesus as the conquering General and himself in the conquering train, sharing in Christ's triumph. "It is a triumph which, Paul is certain, nothing can stop" (Barclay). Fragrance (incense) represents the knowledge of God — "No sense remains in the memory like scent" (Meyer). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-2/)

#### Distinctive Interpretations on "leads us triumphantly":

- **Traditional Reformed** (represented by Ligonier and the older commentaries): Christ parades Paul and the apostles throughout the world as trophies of His victory. Paul is following His General. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/a-fragrance-of-death-and-life)
- **Ellicott/Greek scholarship**: The verb (*thriambeuo*) means "to lead in a triumphal procession" — Paul is led *as a captive* in Christ's train, not as a co-commander. The same verb is used in Colossians 2:15 where Christ "triumphs over" the powers. Paul gives God the glory and "owns that He, as manifested in Christ, had triumphed, and that Apostle and penitent, the faithful and the rebellious, alike took their place in the procession." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik, Pentecostal/charismatic)**: Paul sees himself as "one of the Lord's chief officers" in the triumph, sharing in Jesus' victory, not merely a captive. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-2/)

### v. 15 — *"For we are to God the sweet aroma of Christ among those who are being saved and those who are perishing."*

- **Ellicott**: Paul turns to "the sterner, sadder side of the Roman triumph." Some prisoners were on their way to deliverance, some to perish — and this has its analogue in Christ's triumph. Paul is content to leave souls to God's judgment and continues his work as incense-bearer. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: The same incense smelled wonderful to a victorious Roman but was a stench to a captive about to be executed. In the same way, the gospel is life to some and condemnation to those who reject it. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-2/)

### v. 16 — *"To the one, we are an odor of death and demise; to the other, a fragrance that brings life. And who is qualified for such a task?"*

- **Ellicott**: Paul's "deeply, though unconsciously, poetic imagination" is at work: the incense odour works differently on two classes of prisoners — to some a breath from Paradise, to others "sickly and pestilential, coming as from a charnel house." The question "Who is sufficient?" forces itself on every true teacher aware of such tremendous issues. Paul's answer comes in 2 Corinthians 3:5-6: "Our sufficiency is of God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Spurgeon (Baptist, on vv.15-16)**: Preached an entire sermon on these verses. The gospel produces different effects — like the sun which moistens wax but hardens clay. "It is not the fault of God's truth; it is the fault of those who do not receive it." Ministers are not responsible for their success — "We are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish." Yet the minister's place is weighty: "Who is sufficient for these things?" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Barclay (Daily Study Bible)**: The same gospel is "a perfume from death" to some and "a perfume from life to life" to others — the difference lies in the hearer's response. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/2-corinthians-2.html)

### v. 17 — *"For we are not like so many others, who peddle the word of God for profit. On the contrary, in Christ we speak before God with sincerity, as men sent from God."*

- **Ellicott**: "There is a ring of sadness in the words. Even then the ways of error were manifold, and the way of truth was one." The word for "corrupt" (Greek *kapeleuo*) comes from "huckster" or "tavern-keeper" and implies adulteration like that which such people practised — watering down wine for bigger profits. Paul plays no such "tricks of trade." If the triumph imagery continues: "Our incense, at any rate, is pure. If it brings death it is through no fault of ours. It is not a poisoned perfume." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "Sincerity" (Greek *eilikrineia*) means "pure" — literally "judged by sunlight," meaning something so pure it can be held up to the sun for inspection. Paul spoke "in the sight of God" — God was his first audience. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-2/)
- **Precept Austin (Poole)**: This is a great work — "first to consult the mind and will of God… then faithfully to communicate it… without any vain or corrupt mixtures (which do but adulterate the word preached); then to apply it to the consciences of those that hear us. Who is sufficient for these things?" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-2-commentary)

## Tradition-Specific Distinctives

### Reformed (Ligonier)
- Emphasis on church discipline as a means of grace, with restoration as its proper goal. The church differs from the world in believing "in true grace" and not holding transgressions against repentant sinners forever. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/knowing-satans-designs)
- Christ parades Paul and the apostles as trophies of His victory throughout the world. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/a-fragrance-of-death-and-life)

### Baptist (Spurgeon)
- On vv.15–16: Strong emphasis on divine sovereignty in the different effects of the gospel. The gospel itself is always a "sweet savour" to God regardless of human response. Ministers are not responsible for success but for faithfulness. Yet the task is weighty — "Who is sufficient?" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/2-corinthians-2.html)

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
- In v.14, Paul is portrayed as sharing actively in Christ's triumph, not merely a captive — a co-victor in Jesus' parade. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-2/)
- Strong emphasis on spiritual warfare and Satan's "devices" (vv.8-11), with practical application about being alert to strategies in three areas: the sinner (lust → despair), the church (toleration → undue severity), and the minister (stress that drains effectiveness). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-2/)

---

## Other Views

### Anglican/Older Commentary (Ellicott)
- **On the "lost letter"**: The severe letter Paul mentions (v.4) was a separate letter from 1 Corinthians, now lost — not everything apostles wrote was preserved as Scripture. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)
- **On the offender's identity**: Ellicott identifies the man with the incestuous person of 1 Corinthians 5:1. The singular pronouns and the abrupt question in v.2 point to "the one great offender." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-corinthians-2.html)

### Baptist Historic (Gill)
- Gill holds that the punishment was excommunication; the man repented; the Corinthians were to forgive him and restore him to communion. The "majority" that inflicted punishment indicates church government by the congregation, not a single bishop. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/2.htm)
